Newborn Care

Cross-cradle and other breastfeeding positions: finding your fit

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A small change in how you support your baby can make feeding easier to see, guide and sustain. These four positions offer starting points; the right fit is the one that supports comfortable attachment and effective milk transfer for you and your baby.

Positioning is a skill you can learn together

Breastfeeding does not have to feel instinctive from the first feed. You and your baby are learning how to fit together, and practical support can make a substantial difference. Needing someone to observe a feed is not a sign that you are doing badly.

Cross-cradle is one useful option because it gives your supporting hand a clear role near the baby’s shoulders and neck. Cradle, underarm and side-lying holds offer different ways to manage comfort, recovery from birth and the baby’s size. A position is useful when it supports comfortable attachment and effective feeding, not simply because it looks like a picture.

Set up your support before bringing the baby to the breast

Choose a place where your back, shoulders and arms can relax. In a chair, support your feet if they do not rest comfortably on the floor. On a bed, arrange support for your own back before lifting the baby. A cushion under your arm or lap can reduce strain while you continue to hold and supervise your baby.

Bring the baby close enough that you do not have to bend your neck or lean your breast down toward them. Keep pillows and loose fabric away from the baby’s nose and mouth. Supporting yourself is different from propping a baby in place and leaving them unattended. If discomfort builds through the feed, pause and reset rather than trying to maintain an awkward position.

Use the same alignment checks in every hold

Turn the baby’s whole body toward you, with the ear, shoulder and hip in a comfortable line. A baby should not have to twist the neck to reach the breast. Start with the nose near the nipple and allow the head to tip back slightly as the mouth opens wide and the chin approaches first.

Support the shoulders, upper back and neck without pushing firmly on the back of the head. Keep the nose clear and look for a deep comfortable attachment rather than putting only the nipple into a barely open mouth. If a feed is persistently painful, gently release the suction with a clean finger before trying again, and seek help rather than enduring repeated damage.

Cradle hold: support with the arm on the feeding side

The traditional cradle, sometimes called the Madonna hold, places the baby across your front. For the right breast, use your right arm: rest the head along the forearm or near the bend of the elbow, support the back with the forearm and cup the bottom or upper thigh with the hand. Reverse the arrangement for the left breast.

Keep the baby on their side facing your body, with the lower arm comfortably out of the way rather than wedged between you. Bring the entire baby closer instead of turning only the head. Your free hand can support the breast if helpful, with fingers far enough from the nipple that they do not block a wide mouthful.

When cradle hold needs adjustment

Cradle hold may feel familiar once feeding is going well. It can also be used with a newborn when the head and body are properly supported; independent head control is not a prerequisite. Some families find that another hold provides more precise guidance during the first days or when attachment is difficult.

A baby lying across the abdomen can be uncomfortable after a caesarean birth. Underarm or side-lying feeding may keep pressure away from the incision. Sore or cracked nipples are a reason to assess attachment and other causes of pain, not proof that cradle hold is always forbidden or that changing position alone will resolve the problem.

Underarm, rugby or football hold: make room beside you

Sit with support for your back and an optional cushion along the feeding side. Place the baby beside you, under that arm, with the body close and the legs pointing behind you. On the right breast, the right forearm supports the body while the right hand supports the upper back and neck.

Leave room for the feet rather than pressing them into the chair or bending the baby awkwardly. Bring the nose level with the nipple, wait for a wide mouth and guide the baby closer with support at the shoulders. The free hand can help support the breast. Avoid gripping or pushing the back of the head, which can interfere with the slight backward tilt needed for attachment.

Why underarm feeding may be worth trying

This hold keeps much of the baby’s weight away from a caesarean incision. It can offer a clearer view of the mouth and breast when breasts are large or nipples are flat or inverted. Some parents of small or premature babies find the close support useful, although those babies may also need specialist help with stamina and milk transfer.

Underarm positioning can allow one twin to feed on each side. Learn how to position and support each baby safely before trying simultaneous feeds, and ask another adult for help if useful. None of these circumstances makes one hold compulsory. Comfort, attachment and how well each baby feeds still guide the choice.

Side-lying: face each other without raising the baby on a pillow

Lie on your side with your baby facing you, tummy toward tummy, and keep the baby’s head and body aligned. Arrange a pillow for your own head or support behind your back so it stays well away from the baby’s face. Use your free arm to bring the baby close and support them while they attach.

Do not put a pillow or folded blanket under the baby’s head to lift it toward the breast. Adjust your position and the baby’s whole body instead. Avoid trapping the lower arm or twisting the neck. Remain awake, watch the baby throughout the feed and remove any temporary positioning supports when the feed ends.

Side-lying comfort does not make the feeding space a safe sleep space

Lying on your side may be helpful after a caesarean or difficult birth, when sitting hurts, or when holding a larger baby is tiring. A baby without head control still needs careful alignment and support. Night feeds may feel easier this way, but tiredness also makes it more important to plan what happens if you become sleepy.

After feeding, place the baby on their back in a separate firm, flat infant sleep space without pillows, blankets or soft objects. Do not fall asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. If you are too sleepy to stay alert, ask for help and move the baby to their own sleep space rather than continuing an unsupported feed.

Cross-cradle: use the opposite arm to guide attachment

For the right breast, hold the baby with your left arm. Let the forearm support the body and place the left hand around the upper back and base of the neck, near the shoulders rather than pressing the back of the skull. The baby’s body faces you across your front. Your right hand is then free to support the right breast.

Bring the nose toward the nipple, allow a slight head tilt and wait for the mouth to open wide. Bring the baby close, chin first, using the shoulder and upper-back support. Keep the body aligned as you do so. For the left breast, reverse the arms. A cushion may support your forearm, but your hand still controls the baby’s position.

When cross-cradle can help, and when to ask for more support

Cross-cradle is often useful in the newborn days, for a small baby or when you want more control while learning attachment. A premature baby or a baby who repeatedly slips off may benefit from an observed feed and a tailored plan. Painful or damaged nipples also warrant assessment; the goal is a comfortable deep latch, not holding the baby more tightly.

If the baby has a cleft lip or palate, do not assume side-lying or any general-purpose hold will solve feeding. A cleft lip alone differs from a cleft palate, which can make suction and milk transfer much harder. A cleft or feeding team should individualize position, milk delivery and supplementation if needed; more upright or underarm positions may be considered. Monitor intake and growth while the plan is established.

Judge the result by feeding, comfort and growth

A position that looks tidy can still need adjustment if the baby is not transferring milk or you remain in pain. Ask a midwife, lactation professional or other qualified feeding clinician to watch a whole feed. Describe where it hurts, when the baby loses attachment and which holds you have tried.

Seek prompt help for ongoing nipple injury, repeated difficulty attaching, unexpectedly few wet nappies, poor weight gain or a baby who is too sleepy or weak to feed effectively. Marked illness, breathing difficulty or difficulty waking needs urgent medical care. You can change positions as recovery and your baby’s size change; there is no requirement to master every hold or use the same one at every feed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Keep the baby close and aligned, with support at the neck and shoulders and room for the head to tilt.

Pain or poor milk transfer needs an observed feed, not simply a more forceful hold.

How BeMama can help

Ask someone qualified to watch you try one position and help you adjust it before practising another.

When to seek help

Keep pillows and loose fabric away from the baby’s face. Stay awake during side-lying feeds and return the baby to a separate clear, firm, flat sleep space on their back. Seek prompt help for poor intake or persistent pain.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Cradle uses the arm on the same side as the feeding breast.
  • Cross-cradle uses the opposite arm to guide the shoulders and neck.
  • Underarm feeding can help keep weight away from a caesarean incision.
  • Side-lying requires awake supervision and a separate safe sleep plan.
  • Cleft conditions, prematurity and poor growth need individual feeding support.

Frequently asked questions

Which arm holds the baby in cross-cradle?

Use the opposite arm to the feeding breast: your left arm for the right breast, or your right arm for the left breast.

Should I press the back of my baby’s head toward the nipple?

No. Support the upper back and neck while allowing a slight backward head tilt and a wide mouth opening.

Must a newborn have head control before cradle feeding?

No. A newborn can use cradle hold with appropriate head and body support, though another hold may make attachment easier to guide.

Which position may be comfortable after a caesarean?

Underarm or side-lying feeding may reduce pressure near the incision. Choose the position that is comfortable and supports effective feeding.

Can underarm feeding help with large breasts or flat nipples?

It may improve your view and ability to guide attachment. These features do not make the hold compulsory or guarantee that it will solve every difficulty.

Can I feed twins in underarm holds?

Some parents do. Learn safe positioning for each baby and arrange help if needed before trying simultaneous feeds.

Should I raise my baby’s head on a pillow for side-lying feeding?

No. Keep pillows away from the baby’s face and adjust your own position and the baby’s whole-body alignment instead.

Can my baby stay beside me asleep after a side-lying feed?

Return the baby to their own separate, firm, flat sleep space on their back with no pillows or loose bedding.

Is side-lying always best for a baby with a cleft?

No. Cleft lip and cleft palate affect feeding differently. Ask a specialist feeding team to plan positioning and check milk intake.

What if changing holds does not stop the pain?

Arrange an observed feed and assessment for other causes. Persistent nipple injury or poor milk transfer needs support rather than repeated painful attempts.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
